META.DESCRIPTION: What Locker Protocol protects against, what it does not, and why we chose verifiability over trusted hardware: an honest air-gapped threat model.

HERO.TITLE: The Locker Protocol Threat Model
HERO.SUBTITLE: What we protect against, what we don't, and why we chose verifiability over trusted hardware.

AIR_GAP.TITLE: Air gap by construction, not by policy
AIR_GAP.DESC: The signing device has no USB, no Bluetooth, no network. Requests and signatures cross as QR codes you can see. A property enforced by physics needs no promise.

VERIFY.TITLE: Verifiable beats certified
VERIFY.DESC: The contracts, where your funds actually live, are published and verified on-chain on all 9 networks. Certification asks for your trust; verified contracts don't need it.

NO_DATA.TITLE: No accounts, no servers, no data
NO_DATA.DESC: Nothing to register, nothing shipped, nothing stored about you. A database that doesn't exist cannot leak.

MALWARE.HOW: Keys live on a device with no network connection. Malware on your computer can propose a transaction, but only the offline vault can sign it, after you've read it.

PHISHING.HOW: The vault decodes every request into human-readable fields on a trusted screen before signing. What you sign is what you saw.

SUPPLY.HOW: No hardware is sold, so none can be intercepted. Updates come only through the browser stores, and the contracts holding your funds are verified on-chain.

LOSS.THREAT: Loss or destruction of the device
LOSS.HOW: The paper backup is an encrypted QR code. Print it, store it, restore on any phone with your password.

THEFT.HOW: The vault is encrypted at rest behind your password. But a phone has no certified secure element: against a lab-equipped attacker holding the device, a hardware wallet's chip resists better. On this specific point, a Ledger wins, and we say so.

WRENCH.HOW: No wallet resists physical coercion. The structural answer is M-of-N multisig: no single person, coerced or not, can move the funds.

SE.TITLE: Where a secure element wins
SE.DESC: A certified secure element (CC EAL5+) resists physical key extraction: decapping, glitching, side channels. If your main risk is a sophisticated attacker physically seizing your signer, a dedicated hardware chip defends that scenario better than a phone. We publish this page so you make that trade-off consciously instead of discovering it later.

WHY_SOFTWARE.TITLE: Why software anyway
WHY_SOFTWARE.DESC: In 2023, Ledger Recover demonstrated that firmware decides what a secure element does: the chip protected the seed only until its vendor shipped a way out. A component you cannot inspect protects you only as long as its vendor chooses to. We prefer properties you can check to promises you must trust.

CREATOR_STORY.TITLE: Why Locker Exists
CREATOR_STORY.CONTENT_P1: Every year, billions of dollars in crypto assets are stolen - not because blockchains are insecure, but because the devices used to sign transactions are compromised. Malware silently alters transaction payloads before they reach your hardware wallet, and by the time you confirm, it's already too late.
CREATOR_STORY.CONTENT_P2: Existing solutions all share the same critical flaw: they require a direct connection (USB, Bluetooth, or software bridge) between the signing device and an internet-connected machine. That connection is the attack surface.
CREATOR_STORY.CONTENT_P3: Locker was built from the ground up to eliminate that single point of failure. By physically isolating the keystore via a true Air-Gap and verifying exact transaction payloads on a completely offline device, it ensures that even on a fully compromised computer, attackers cannot alter or intercept your signatures.
CREATOR_STORY.CONTENT_P4: The smart contracts are 100% open-source. Clone them, audit them, deploy them yourself. No trust required - only math.

FAQ.TITLE: Frequently Asked Questions
FAQ.A1: Locker Protocol is a complete, free ecosystem to secure your crypto. It combines locking Smart Contracts (by time or price condition) with an air-gapped offline Vault compatible with Web3. Each user deploys their own contract - no proxy, no admin key - and remains 100% owner.
FAQ.A2: Yes. Deploying your Locker and using the interface are free: the only cost is the blockchain network's gas, with no platform fee, no subscription and no percentage taken from locked assets. The browser extension and the Vault are free too; swaps, bridges and Hyperliquid orders made from the extension carry a small fee (at most 0.25%, and 0.05% on Hyperliquid), always shown before you sign.
FAQ.A3: The Vault is an application installed on a dedicated device kept permanently offline (Airplane Mode). Your private keys are generated and stored locally, never exposed to the Internet. Communication with the online app is done exclusively via QR codes - no USB, Bluetooth or WiFi.
FAQ.A4: Beyond classic time-based locking, Locker Protocol integrates with Uniswap V2/V3 on-chain oracles. You can create a conditional lock: your tokens only unlock when the market price reaches a defined target. The smart contract checks liquidity pools in real time.
FAQ.Q5: Do I need a dedicated device for the Vault?
FAQ.A5: For maximum security, yes - an old reset smartphone or tablet is enough. You install the Vault, switch to Airplane Mode, and the device stays permanently offline. For testing, you can also use it on your main machine.
FAQ.A6: You define an M-of-N threshold: for example 2 out of 3 signers must approve each action. Signatures are collected offline via QR codes. Once the threshold is reached, any wallet can submit the transaction and pay gas once for the entire group.
FAQ.Q7: What happens if I lose my offline device?
FAQ.A7: When creating the wallet, a 12 or 24-word recovery phrase is provided. Write it on paper and store it safely. If your device is lost or destroyed, install the Vault on a new offline device and import your phrase - all your keys are restored.
FAQ.Q8: What happens if your site shuts down?
FAQ.A8: The interface is just a façade to interact with the blockchain. It holds no funds and no keys. The smart contracts are published on GitHub and verified on-chain, so you can always reach your Locker directly through a block explorer. Your funds are on the blockchain, not with us.
FAQ.Q9: Can signers be changed after deployment?
FAQ.A9: Yes. The SignerManager contract allows adding, removing signers or changing the security threshold at any time. These administrative actions themselves require multi-signature approval from the current quorum.
FAQ.Q10: What is the encrypted Paper Wallet?
FAQ.A10: The Paper Wallet uses AES-256 encryption protected by your password. Even if someone finds your paper, they cannot read the keys without the password. Scan the printed QR code with a new air-gapped device to instantly restore your wallet.
FAQ.Q11: Do my private keys ever travel via Bluetooth or USB?
FAQ.A11: Never. The Vault uses no Bluetooth, NFC, WiFi, or USB. The only communication method is scanning animated QR codes (BC-UR protocol). No malware can cross this physical barrier.
FAQ.A12: Your air-gapped Vault connects to MetaMask via QR codes. You can interact with any Web3 dApp (Uniswap, Aave, etc.) while maintaining total physical isolation. Private keys never leave the offline device.
FAQ.Q13: If tokens are sent to the contract by mistake, are they lost?
FAQ.A13: No. The protocol includes a Token Rescue function. Authorized signers can recover mistakenly sent tokens via a multi-signature action validated by the quorum.
FAQ.A14: Locker Protocol is 100% EVM-compatible and deployed on: Ethereum, Arbitrum, Base, Optimism, Polygon, BNB Chain, Avalanche and Linea.
FAQ.A15: The smart contracts are: they are published on GitHub and verified on-chain, so any expert can read every line that holds your funds. The browser extension ships reproducible builds: its store packages can be rebuilt bit for bit from the source archive given to store reviewers.

SAFEST.Q: What is the safest crypto wallet extension?
SAFEST.A: The one that keeps the private key off the computer. A browser extension that stores the key, even encrypted, can be emptied by malware, a malicious extension or a phishing signature. Pairing an extension with a hardware wallet, or using one whose key lives on an air-gapped device, removes that risk: the computer only ever sees public addresses and signed transactions.

METAMASK.Q: Is MetaMask still the best wallet extension in 2027?
METAMASK.A: It is still the extension most EVM dApps are built around, and many others answer to the same interface. Whether it is the best depends on what you hold: MetaMask keeps its key in the browser unless you pair a hardware wallet, and other extensions cover chains, fees or a security model it does not.

LEDGER.Q: Which wallet extensions work with a Ledger?
LEDGER.A: Most of the extensions in this list can sign with a Ledger device, as the table shows. A Ledger keeps the key on a USB or Bluetooth device you plug in. An air-gapped wallet goes one step further: the signing device never connects to the computer at all and exchanges data only through QR codes.

AIR_GAPPED.A: A wallet whose private key sits on a device that never connects to any network: no Wi-Fi, no USB, no Bluetooth. Transactions travel to it and back as QR codes, so nothing on the internet can reach the key. Locker Vault turns a spare phone into one, for free.

ONE_WALLET.Q: Can one extension replace MetaMask, Phantom and Keplr?
ONE_WALLET.A: Increasingly, yes. Multichain extensions now cover EVM chains, Solana and Cosmos from one recovery phrase. What matters is whether your dApps detect them: Locker Protocol Wallet answers the connect flows built for MetaMask, Keplr, TronLink and Freighter, and appears in the Wallet Standard list on Solana, Sui and Aptos.

FEES.A: Installing and holding is free with every wallet here. Built-in swaps and bridges usually carry a fee added by the wallet on top of network costs, and it varies from one wallet to another. Locker Protocol Wallet adds at most 0.25% to swaps and bridges and 0.05% to Hyperliquid orders, shown before you sign.

DOGECOIN.SUBTITLE: DOGE in a Chrome and Brave extension, on the same engine that signs Bitcoin - while the key that signs stays on a device with no network connection at all.

C1.TITLE: The Bitcoin engine, parameterised
C1.TEXT: Dogecoin rides the same UTXO engine as Bitcoin, with its own parameters and its own legacy signing: one implementation, proven once, rather than a copy that drifts.

C2.TITLE: A fee above the amount is refused
C2.TEXT: Dogecoin fees are quoted per kilobyte and its amounts are large, which is exactly the shape that turns a transfer into a donation to a miner. A send whose fee exceeds what it moves is refused before the ceremony, with no way to arm it.

C3.TITLE: Dust is named, not hidden
C3.TEXT: An output below the network’s dust limit is pointed out on the offline device before you approve it, because a transaction that cannot relay is a transaction that fails after you have signed.

C4.TITLE: The same recovery phrase
C4.TEXT: The Dogecoin address is derived from the phrase you already wrote down, on Dogecoin’s own path. One phrase, every chain, one backup.

Q1.Q: Can I keep DOGE on an air-gapped wallet for free?
Q1.A: Yes. The Locker Protocol Wallet is a free browser extension, and the key is held by the Locker Vault - a free application you install on a spare phone or laptop and keep offline. There is no hardware to buy.

Q2.Q: How does the signature reach the browser?
Q2.A: Optically. The extension shows the transaction as a QR code, the offline device scans it, you approve it there, and it shows the signature back as another QR code. No cable, no Bluetooth, no pairing.

Q3.Q: Does it protect me from a fee mistake?
Q3.A: A send whose fee is larger than the amount it moves is refused outright, and outputs below the dust limit are named on the review screen before you sign.

Q4.Q: Do I need a separate backup for Dogecoin?
Q4.A: No. It comes from the same recovery phrase as your other chains.

META.TITLE: Air-Gapped Ethereum Wallet, a MetaMask Alternative
META.DESCRIPTION: An Ethereum extension that dApps detect like MetaMask, while the key stays on an offline device: calldata decoded, every signature approved by QR code.

ETHEREUM.TITLE: An Ethereum wallet whose key is on another device
ETHEREUM.SUBTITLE: Every dApp you already use, answering the standard Web3 API, with the key on a machine that has no network. The transaction is decoded, checked and shown to you twice: in the browser, and again on the device that actually signs it.

C1.TITLE: A drop-in wallet, not a plugin to learn
C1.TEXT: It announces itself over EIP-6963, so sites list it beside the wallets they already offer. Transactions, personal_sign, EIP-712 typed data and EIP-5792 batched calls all go through the same optical ceremony.

C2.TITLE: The calldata is read before you sign
C2.TEXT: An approval, a transfer, a swap: the call is decoded into what it does and who it lets spend, with the known-phishing list checked from a snapshot that ships with the extension - no lookup, no leak of where you are going.

C3.TITLE: A local model, not a cloud service
C3.TEXT: A small model runs on your machine to flag a request that does not look like what it claims to be. It never leaves the device and it never gates: it explains, you decide, and the offline device still shows the truth.

C4.TITLE: Allowances you can take back
C4.TEXT: A token allowance you granted once can be revoked from the wallet, through the same review and the same offline signature.

Q1.Q: Is it a MetaMask alternative?
Q1.A: It answers the same standard interface, so dApps treat it as an ordinary wallet. The difference is where the key is: on a separate device with no network, instead of in the browser.

Q2.Q: Does every dApp work with it?
Q2.A: It implements the standard Web3 provider API and announces itself over EIP-6963, which is how modern sites discover wallets. Nearly two hundred real sites are driven end to end by the test suite on every release.

Q3.Q: What about typed data and batched calls?
Q3.A: EIP-712 typed data is decoded field by field on the offline device, and EIP-5792 batched calls are shown as the list of calls they are.

Q4.A: Yes, both the extension and the Vault, with reproducible builds published for the stores. Swaps and bridges made from the extension add at most 0.25%, shown before you sign.

META.TITLE: Air-Gapped Wallet for Arbitrum, Base, Polygon and BNB
META.DESCRIPTION: One offline key for Arbitrum, Base, Polygon, Optimism, BNB Chain, Avalanche, Linea and any EVM chain you add, with every signature approved by QR code.

EVM_NETWORKS.TITLE: Every EVM network, one offline key
EVM_NETWORKS.SUBTITLE: Arbitrum, Base, Polygon, Optimism, BNB Chain, Avalanche and Linea run the same machine as Ethereum, so they share an address, a key and a review screen. What changes between them is the network you are pointed at - and that is never changed for you.

C1.TITLE: One address across all of them
C1.TEXT: The same account, derived once from your recovery phrase, holds funds on every EVM network. Adding a network adds a place to look, never a second thing to back up.

C2.TITLE: A site cannot move your network in silence
C2.TEXT: Switching the active network is a global act - it moves every other connected tab and the wallet’s own screens - so a site asking for it raises a consent card every time, and a tab you are not looking at cannot raise it at all.

C3.TITLE: Point a network at your own node
C3.TEXT: Every network, bundled ones included, can be pointed at an endpoint you choose and put back to its default afterwards. The wallet refuses endpoints that are not public https, which is what keeps a site from aiming it at your local network.

C4.TITLE: Add a network, with what it costs shown
C4.TEXT: A site may ask to add a network. You see the chain id, the name and the RPC it wants before anything is fetched, and the endpoint is probed only after you have agreed.

EVM_NETWORKS.FAQ_TITLE: EVM networks wallet: questions people ask

Q1.Q: Which EVM networks are included?
Q1.A: Ethereum, Arbitrum, Base, Polygon, Optimism, BNB Chain, Avalanche, Linea, Hyperliquid’s EVM and Robinhood Chain, plus any network you add yourself.

Q2.Q: Do I need a different key per network?
Q2.A: No. One account from one recovery phrase works on all of them.

Q3.Q: Can a dApp switch my network without asking?
Q3.A: No. The active network is global, so every switch raises a consent card, and a background tab cannot raise one at all.

Q4.Q: Can I use my own RPC endpoint?
Q4.A: Yes, on any network including the bundled ones, and you can restore the default at any time.

META.TITLE: Hyperliquid Wallet: Trade Perps With Offline Keys
META.DESCRIPTION: Trade Hyperliquid perpetuals from a browser extension: positions, funding and PnL in the wallet, and the trading agent authorised on an offline device.

HYPERLIQUID.TITLE: Hyperliquid perpetuals, with the key on another device
HYPERLIQUID.SUBTITLE: Balances, positions, funding and orders inside the extension - and the authorisation that makes trading possible signed on a device with no network, for a period you can see and that ends on its own.

C1.TITLE: The agent is signed offline, and it expires
C1.TEXT: Trading on Hyperliquid runs through an agent key. That authorisation is signed on the offline device like any other transaction, it is valid for thirty days, and the wallet shows when it runs out instead of renewing it behind your back.

C2.TITLE: Positions, funding and PnL, read in place
C2.TEXT: Open positions, their funding and their profit and loss are shown in the wallet, so you are not moving between an interface and a wallet that disagree.

C3.TITLE: Spot and perps, and the bridge between them
C3.TEXT: HYPE moves between HyperCore and HyperEVM, and the wallet does that transfer explicitly rather than leaving you to work out which side your balance is on.

C4.TITLE: The fee is stated
C4.TEXT: What the wallet charges on a trade is written down in the interface and in the terms, not discovered in a quote.

Q1.Q: Can I trade Hyperliquid perpetuals with an air-gapped key?
Q1.A: Yes. The agent authorisation that trading needs is signed on the offline device; orders then go out under that agent, which expires after thirty days.

Q2.Q: Does the extension show my positions?
Q2.A: Yes - open positions, funding and PnL, read from Hyperliquid and shown in the wallet.

Q3.Q: What happens when the agent expires?
Q3.A: Trading stops until you sign a new one. The wallet tells you the date rather than renewing silently.

Q4.A: Yes: once you approve it, 0.05% of each order goes to the wallet as a builder fee, on top of Hyperliquid's own fees. It is stated in the interface before you sign and in the terms of use.

META.TITLE: Air-Gapped Litecoin Wallet (LTC)
META.DESCRIPTION: Hold LTC in a browser extension whose private key never touches your computer. Native SegWit, a fee checked against the amount, signed offline.

LITECOIN.TITLE: A Litecoin wallet whose key is on another device
LITECOIN.SUBTITLE: LTC in a Chrome and Brave extension, on the same engine that signs Bitcoin - parameterised, never duplicated - while the key that signs stays on a device with no network.

C1.TITLE: The Bitcoin engine, parameterised
C1.TEXT: Litecoin is not a second implementation: it is the same UTXO engine, the same PSBT, the same review screen, with this chain’s own parameters. What has been proven on Bitcoin holds here, instead of being written twice and tested once.

C2.TITLE: A fee above the amount is refused
C2.TEXT: The classic mistake on these chains is a fee-per-kilobyte read as a fee-per-byte, which turns a small transfer into a large donation to a miner. A send whose fee exceeds what it moves is refused outright, and there is no checkbox to arm it.

C3.TITLE: Signed off the machine
C3.TEXT: The unsigned transaction leaves as a QR code and comes back signed. The offline device shows the outputs, the fee as a share of the amount, and any output below the dust limit - then signs, and never sees a network.

C4.TITLE: The same recovery phrase
C4.TEXT: The Litecoin address comes from the phrase you already have, on Litecoin’s own derivation path, with ltc1 native SegWit addresses.

Q1.Q: Is the Locker Protocol Wallet a Litecoin hardware wallet?
Q1.A: It is the same idea without the hardware: the key lives on a second device you already own, kept offline, and signs through QR codes. There is nothing to buy, nothing to plug in, and the build is reproducible.

Q2.Q: Which Litecoin addresses does it use?
Q2.A: Native SegWit (ltc1), derived from your recovery phrase on Litecoin’s own path.

Q3.Q: Can it send to a legacy L-address?
Q3.A: Yes. The review screen on the offline device names every output and the fee before you approve it.

Q4.A: No. The extension and the Vault are free, and neither carries an account or any telemetry.

META.TITLE: Robinhood Chain Token Lockers by Locker Protocol
META.DESCRIPTION: Lock ERC-20 tokens, WETH, USDG and Robinhood Stock Tokens on Robinhood Chain, with time locks and price-conditioned releases in verified smart contracts.

ROBINHOOD_CHAIN.TITLE: Official Token Lockers on Robinhood Chain
ROBINHOOD_CHAIN.SUBTITLE: Securely lock WETH, USDG, and official Robinhood Stock Tokens. Create high-security time-locks and price-conditioned release vaults directly on the Robinhood EVM Layer-2 network.

C1.TITLE: Time-Locked Vaults
C1.TEXT: Create secure vesting vaults and locks. Lock any standard ERC-20 assets on Robinhood Chain until a specified date and time, protected by smart contracts verified on-chain.

C2.TITLE: Price-Conditioned Releases
C2.TEXT: Lock tokens until an asset reaches a specific target price, calculated dynamically using Uniswap V2 pairs and Uniswap V3 pools on Robinhood Chain.

C3.TITLE: Verified Stock Tokens
C3.TEXT: Official registry verification for Robinhood Stock Tokens (AAPL, NVDA, TSLA, MSFT, META, SPY, QQQ). It prevents token spoofing.

Q1.Q: How do I connect to the Robinhood Chain on Locker Protocol?
Q1.A: Simply click the network selector modal in the upper right corner of the Locker Protocol application and select 'Robinhood Chain'. If the network is not configured in your MetaMask or other EVM wallet, the application will prompt you to automatically add and configure the chain ID 4663 network configuration.

Q2.Q: Can I lock Robinhood Stock Tokens (AAPL, NVDA, TSLA, etc.)?
Q2.A: Yes. The official Robinhood Stock Tokens are standard ERC-20 contracts on the Robinhood Chain. Locker Protocol recognizes their canonical contract addresses, displays verified status badges, and supports creation of secure temporal and price-conditioned locks for these assets.

Q3.Q: How are prices calculated for LP pairs and price-conditioned locks?
Q3.A: Locker Protocol utilizes a dynamic on-chain PriceCalculator contract that interacts directly with Uniswap V2 and Uniswap V3 pricing pools. The interface integrates the DexScreener API and on-chain factory registry checks to resolve pricing structures cleanly.

META.TITLE: Air-Gapped Solana Wallet (SOL and SPL Tokens)
META.DESCRIPTION: Hold SOL and SPL tokens with the key on an offline device. Solana apps connect as usual, and each transaction is simulated before you sign it by QR code.

SOLANA.TITLE: A Solana wallet whose key is on another device
SOLANA.SUBTITLE: SOL and the SPL tokens you hold, in a Chrome and Brave extension that Solana apps connect to the way they connect to any other - while the key that signs stays on a device with no network.

C1.TITLE: Simulated before it is signed
C1.TEXT: A Solana transaction is a list of instructions against programs, and what it will do is not obvious from its bytes. It is simulated first, and what the simulation says about your balances is shown before the ceremony starts.

C2.TITLE: The programs are named
C2.TEXT: The instructions that belong to known programs are named rather than shown as opaque data, and anything the wallet cannot name is said to be unnamed instead of being dressed up as safe.

C3.TITLE: Sign in with Solana
C3.TEXT: SIWS message signing works through the same offline device, so logging into an app costs a QR scan and no key ever comes near the browser.

C4.TITLE: SPL tokens appear as they are held
C4.TEXT: There is no list to curate: a mint shows up when your account holds it, with the balance the chain reports.

Q1.Q: Do Solana apps connect to it?
Q1.A: Yes. It presents the wallet interface Solana apps expect, so it appears in their picker and connects like any other wallet.

Q2.Q: Where is the Solana private key?
Q2.A: On a second device with no network - the Locker Vault. The extension holds the public key and the address only.

Q3.A: Yes, and they appear the moment the account holds them; there is no list to add to.

Q4.Q: Is the transaction checked before I approve it?
Q4.A: It is simulated, and the offline device decodes the instructions again from the bytes it is about to sign.

META.TITLE: Air-Gapped Stellar Wallet for XLM and USDC
META.DESCRIPTION: Hold XLM and issued assets such as USDC with the key on an offline device. Memos, trustlines and path payments are shown in full before you sign.

STELLAR.TITLE: A Stellar wallet whose key is on another device
STELLAR.SUBTITLE: XLM and the assets issued on Stellar, in a Chrome and Brave extension, with the key on a device that has no network. On this chain an asset is a code AND an issuer, and this wallet says which issuer you are trusting.

C1.TITLE: The memo is part of the payment
C1.TEXT: A Stellar payment to an exchange without its memo is a payment nobody can attribute. The memo is treated as part of the recipient and always shown, never folded away when empty.

C2.TITLE: An asset is a code and an issuer
C2.TEXT: Anybody can issue "USDC". A token that borrows a known code from another issuer is called out, and the offline device re-derives that judgement from the bytes it is signing rather than trusting the browser.

C3.TITLE: Trustlines, with what they cost
C3.TEXT: Holding an issued asset means signing a trustline, and a trustline locks reserve. The amount being locked is named before you approve it.

C4.TITLE: Swaps over the Stellar DEX
C4.TEXT: Trades route through path payments on the chain’s own order books - the only rail Stellar has, and the reason it swaps without bridging.

Q1.Q: Can I hold USDC on Stellar with it?
Q1.A: Yes, once the trustline exists - and the wallet opens one from the same offline ceremony, showing the reserve it locks first.

Q2.Q: Does it handle memos?
Q2.A: Yes, as part of the recipient. The memo is always displayed on the offline device before signing.

Q3.Q: What protects me from a fake issuer?
Q3.A: The asset is identified by code and issuer together. An asset wearing a known code from an unknown issuer is flagged, on both the extension and the offline device.

Q4.A: On a second device with no network. Every signature crosses as a QR code.

META.TITLE: Air-Gapped Sui Wallet (SUI and Coins)
META.DESCRIPTION: Hold SUI and its coins in a browser extension whose private key never touches your computer. Sui apps connect via the Wallet Standard, signed offline.

SUI.TITLE: A Sui wallet whose key is on another device
SUI.SUBTITLE: SUI and the coins you hold, in a Chrome and Brave extension that Sui apps discover through the Wallet Standard - while the key that signs stays on a device with no network.

C1.TITLE: The transaction block is decoded
C1.TEXT: A Sui transaction is a programmable block of commands over objects. The offline device decodes that block and names what it moves, rather than showing you a hash to trust.

C2.TITLE: Sponsored gas is shown as such
C2.TEXT: When an app pays the gas for you, the transaction has two parties and only one of them is you. The review says so, because "who pays" changes what you are agreeing to.

C3.TITLE: Coins, as the chain reports them
C3.TEXT: Coin types appear with the balances the node returns; a coin you hold is a row, not a list entry somebody has to maintain.

C4.TITLE: Discovered like any other wallet
C4.TEXT: The Wallet Standard announcement is what Sui apps read, so the extension appears in their picker beside the others - measured against the real sites.

Q1.Q: Do Sui apps connect to it?
Q1.A: Yes, through the Wallet Standard that Sui apps use to discover wallets.

Q2.Q: Where is the Sui private key?
Q2.A: On a second device with no network connection. The extension never holds it.

Q3.Q: What does the offline device show for a Sui transaction?
Q3.A: The decoded transaction block - the commands, what they move, and whether the gas is sponsored by someone else.

Q4.Q: Does it need its own recovery phrase?
Q4.A: No. The Sui address is derived from the phrase you already have.

META.TITLE: Air-Gapped Tron Wallet (TRX and USDT-TRC20)
META.DESCRIPTION: Hold TRX and TRC-20 tokens such as USDT with the key on an offline device. Tron apps connect as they do with TronLink, and you sign by QR code.

TRON.TITLE: A Tron wallet whose key is on another device
TRON.SUBTITLE: TRX and TRC-20 tokens - USDT above all - in a Chrome and Brave extension, with the key on a device that has no network. The fee limit and the permission being used are named before you sign, not after.

C1.TITLE: USDT on Tron, held offline
C1.TEXT: The chain most people use for stablecoin transfers, with the key kept on a second device. The token, the amount and the recipient are shown on that device, from the transaction bytes.

C2.TITLE: The fee limit is shown
C2.TEXT: A Tron contract call carries a fee limit, and it is the field that quietly decides how much energy a call may burn. The review names it rather than leaving it in the raw data.

C3.TITLE: Message signing, both versions
C3.TEXT: TIP-191 message signing is supported in the version apps use today and the legacy one they sometimes still send, with the digest computed byte for byte as the reference implementation does.

C4.TITLE: Tron apps connect as usual
C4.TEXT: The extension answers the interface Tron apps expect, so SunSwap and the rest list it beside the wallets they already support.

Q1.Q: Can I hold USDT-TRC20 with it?
Q1.A: Yes. USDT and the other TRC-20 tokens are held by the same account, and every transfer is signed on the offline device.

Q2.Q: Does it work with Tron dApps?
Q2.A: Yes - it presents the interface those sites expect and appears in their wallet picker.

Q3.Q: What is shown before I sign?
Q3.A: The recipient, the amount, the token, the fee limit and the permission id, read from the transaction on the offline device.

Q4.Q: Do I need a separate seed phrase?
Q4.A: No. The Tron address comes from the same recovery phrase as your other chains.

META.TITLE: Air-Gapped XRP Ledger Wallet (XRP, RLUSD)
META.DESCRIPTION: Hold XRP and tokens such as RLUSD with the key on an offline device. Reserve, destination tag and trust lines are read from the ledger before you sign.

XRP_LEDGER.TITLE: An XRP Ledger wallet whose key is on another device
XRP_LEDGER.SUBTITLE: XRP and the tokens issued on the ledger, in a Chrome and Brave extension - while the key that signs stays on a device with no network. The XRP Ledger is the network; XRP is the asset that lives on it, and this wallet says which of the two is leaving your account.

C1.TITLE: The reserve is read, not guessed
C1.TEXT: An XRPL account cannot spend below its reserve, and the reserve is a figure the validators vote on - so it is read from the ledger rather than written into the software. What the send screen offers as your maximum is what the chain will actually let go.

C2.TITLE: The destination tag is part of the recipient
C2.TEXT: An exchange address without its tag is a payment nobody can attribute. The account itself says whether it requires one, so the warning comes from the chain rather than from a list of exchanges that is wrong the day it goes stale.

C3.TITLE: Issued tokens, by currency AND issuer
C3.TEXT: On this ledger an asset is a couple: a currency code and the account that issues it. Two issuers may legitimately use the same code, so a token that borrows a known symbol from another issuer is called out - on the extension and again on the offline device, which re-derives that verdict from the signed bytes rather than believing what the browser said.

C4.TITLE: Refused before you walk to the Vault
C4.TEXT: Sending an issued token needs a trust line on both sides, room left under the recipient’s limit, an issuer that has not frozen the line, and a fee that is still XRP. All of it is checked before the ceremony starts, so a refusal costs two reads instead of a walk to another device and two QR scans.

XRP_LEDGER.FAQ_TITLE: XRP Ledger wallet: questions people ask

Q1.Q: Can I hold RLUSD with the Locker Protocol Wallet?
Q1.A: Yes. RLUSD and any issued token on the XRP Ledger appear once a trust line exists, and a trust line can be opened from the wallet - with the reserve it locks and the ceiling you are signing for named before you approve it.

Q2.Q: Where is my XRP private key?
Q2.A: On a second device with no network connection - the Locker Vault. The extension holds the address only, and every signature is approved on that device by QR code.

Q3.A: Yes, as part of the recipient rather than as an optional field. The wallet also reads whether the destination account requires a tag, and refuses to stage a payment without one when it does.

Q4.Q: Do XRPL apps connect to it?
Q4.A: Not yet, and that is deliberate: no injection standard has settled on the XRP Ledger, so the wallet ships the chain without pretending to a dApp surface. Sending, receiving and tokens work; connecting a site does not.

DAPPS_BITCOIN.Q: Do dApps that support {{name}} work with Locker Protocol Wallet?
DAPPS_BITCOIN.A: Bitcoin sites that support Unisat or the sats-connect standard find Locker Protocol Wallet, which announces itself the way those wallets do and never takes the place of a wallet already installed.

DAPPS_SUI.Q: Do dApps that support {{name}} work with Locker Protocol Wallet?

DAPPS_TRON.Q: Do dApps that support {{name}} work with Locker Protocol Wallet?
