AIR_GAPPED_WALLET.NAME: Air-gapped wallet
AIR_GAPPED_WALLET.TITLE: What is an air-gapped wallet?

META.TITLE: What Is an Air-Gapped Wallet? How Offline Signing Works
META.DESCRIPTION: An air-gapped wallet keeps the private key on a device with no network at all. Learn how it signs by QR code and why malware cannot reach the key.

AIR_GAPPED_WALLET.DEF: An air-gapped wallet keeps the private key on a device that is physically cut off from every network: no Wi-Fi, no mobile data, no Bluetooth, no cable. Transactions reach it and leave it as QR codes, so the key itself never travels.
AIR_GAPPED_WALLET.WHY: Most thefts from crypto wallets happen remotely: malware on the computer, a malicious browser extension, a drainer script on a fake site. All of them need a path to the key. On an air-gapped device there is no such path, only a camera that reads a QR code and a screen that shows one.
AIR_GAPPED_WALLET.LOCKER: Locker Protocol Wallet splits the job in two. The browser extension shows balances and talks to dApps but holds no key. The key lives in Locker Vault, a free app on a spare phone or tablet that stays offline, which decodes each request, shows it to you, and signs only after you approve it.

Q1.Q: Is an air-gapped wallet the same as a hardware wallet?
Q1.A: Not quite. A hardware wallet is a dedicated device, usually linked by USB or Bluetooth. An air-gapped wallet has no data link at all and exchanges transactions by QR code or memory card. Some hardware wallets can work air-gapped; Locker Vault is an air-gapped wallet that runs on a phone you already own.

Q2.Q: Can an air-gapped wallet use dApps?
Q2.A: Yes. The online side, here the browser extension, connects to the site and prepares the transaction. The offline device only signs: you approve on its screen and scan the signed answer back.

COLD_WALLET.NAME: Cold wallet
COLD_WALLET.TITLE: What is a cold wallet?

META.TITLE: What Is a Cold Wallet? Cold vs Hot Crypto Storage
META.DESCRIPTION: A cold wallet keeps the private key away from any device connected to the internet. See how cold storage differs from a hot wallet and what it protects.

COLD_WALLET.DEF: A cold wallet is any way of holding crypto where the private key stays on a device that is not connected to the internet. The opposite is a hot wallet, whose key sits on an online computer or phone.
COLD_WALLET.WHY: An online key can be copied by anyone who compromises the device holding it, from anywhere in the world. A cold key has to be reached physically. That is why exchanges keep most customer funds in cold storage, and why long-term holders move their savings there.
COLD_WALLET.LOCKER: Locker Vault turns a spare phone into cold storage: set it up, switch off every radio and keep it offline. Unlike a paper wallet, it can still sign: the browser extension sends each transaction to it as a QR code, and it answers the same way.

Q1.Q: Is a cold wallet safer than a hot wallet?
Q1.A: Against remote attacks, yes, because there is no network path to the key. It does not protect a recovery phrase written where others can read it, and it does not stop you approving a bad transaction, which is why the offline device should show you exactly what you sign.

Q2.Q: Do I need to buy a device for cold storage?
Q2.A: No. A dedicated hardware wallet is one option. Another is an old phone kept permanently offline, running a signing app such as Locker Vault, which is free.

HOT_WALLET.NAME: Hot wallet
HOT_WALLET.TITLE: What is a hot wallet?

META.TITLE: What Is a Hot Wallet? Risks of Online Crypto Wallets
META.DESCRIPTION: A hot wallet keeps the private key on an internet-connected device, like most browser extensions. Learn the risks and how to keep the key offline instead.

HOT_WALLET.DEF: A hot wallet is a crypto wallet whose private key is stored on a device connected to the internet: a browser extension, a mobile app, a desktop app or an exchange account. It is convenient because it can sign instantly.
HOT_WALLET.WHY: Convenience is also the weakness. The key, even encrypted, sits on a machine that runs other software and visits websites. A malicious extension, a clipboard hijacker or a fake update can steal it, and a stolen key can be emptied in seconds, with no way to reverse it.
HOT_WALLET.LOCKER: Locker Protocol Wallet looks and works like a browser wallet, but it is not a hot wallet: the extension stores no private key. Signing happens on Locker Vault, an offline device, so what an attacker can reach in the browser cannot move your funds.

Q1.Q: Is MetaMask a hot wallet?
Q1.A: Used on its own, yes: MetaMask keeps an encrypted copy of your key in the browser. Paired with a hardware wallet, the key stays on the device and MetaMask only prepares transactions.

Q2.Q: Should I stop using hot wallets?
Q2.A: A hot wallet holding a small balance for daily use is a reasonable trade-off. Savings belong on a key that never touches an online device.

HARDWARE_WALLET.NAME: Hardware wallet
HARDWARE_WALLET.TITLE: What is a hardware wallet?

META.TITLE: What Is a Hardware Wallet? And a Free Alternative
META.DESCRIPTION: A hardware wallet is a device that stores your private key and signs offline. Learn how Ledger and Trezor work, their limits, and a free air-gapped option.

HARDWARE_WALLET.DEF: A hardware wallet is a small dedicated device that generates and stores a private key and signs transactions inside itself. Ledger, Trezor and Keystone are well-known brands. The computer prepares the transaction; the device signs it.
HARDWARE_WALLET.WHY: Keeping the key on separate hardware means a compromised computer cannot read it. The limits are practical: the device costs money, most models connect by USB or Bluetooth, the screen is small, and some cannot fully decode what a dApp asks you to sign, which leads to blind signing.
HARDWARE_WALLET.LOCKER: Locker Protocol Wallet does not work with Ledger or Trezor. It reaches the same goal another way: the key lives on Locker Vault, a free app on a phone that stays offline, with a full-size screen to read the transaction and no cable or Bluetooth link, only QR codes.

Q1.Q: Is a phone as safe as a hardware wallet?
Q1.A: A phone that is online is not. A phone that is reset, set up as a signer and never reconnected removes the network path that remote attacks need. Against someone who physically takes the device, a hardware wallet's secure chip does more; on the Vault, the keys are encrypted with your master password.

Q2.Q: Do I need a hardware wallet to use Locker Protocol Wallet?
Q2.A: No. The Vault app takes its place. You need the browser extension and a spare phone or tablet to keep offline.

CRYPTO_WALLET.NAME: Crypto wallet
CRYPTO_WALLET.TITLE: What is a crypto wallet?

META.TITLE: What Is a Crypto Wallet? Keys, Addresses and Types
META.DESCRIPTION: A crypto wallet does not hold coins: it holds the keys that control them. Learn how wallets work, the main types, and how to choose one that fits you.

CRYPTO_WALLET.DEF: A crypto wallet is software or hardware that holds the keys to your funds on a blockchain. The coins themselves stay on the chain; the wallet keeps the private key that proves they are yours and uses it to sign transactions.
CRYPTO_WALLET.WHY: Whoever holds the key controls the funds, so the real question behind any wallet is where the key lives and who can reach it. A custodial wallet, such as an exchange account, keeps it for you. A non-custodial wallet leaves it with you, on an online device (hot) or an offline one (cold).
CRYPTO_WALLET.LOCKER: Locker Protocol Wallet is a non-custodial browser wallet with a difference: the extension you use every day holds no key. It shows balances on EVM networks, Solana, Bitcoin, Cosmos, Tron, Sui, Aptos, Stellar and the XRP Ledger, and sends every signature to Locker Vault, an offline device.

Q1.Q: What is the safest type of crypto wallet?
Q1.A: For money you cannot afford to lose, one whose key never touches an internet-connected device: a hardware wallet or an air-gapped signer. The best wallet is also one that shows you clearly what you are signing.

Q2.Q: Can one wallet hold several cryptocurrencies?
Q2.A: Yes. Multichain wallets derive keys for many chains from one recovery phrase. Check which chains a wallet really supports, and whether the dApps you use can connect to it.

BROWSER_EXTENSION_WALLET.NAME: Browser extension wallet
BROWSER_EXTENSION_WALLET.TITLE: What is a browser extension wallet?

META.TITLE: What Is a Browser Extension Wallet? How It Works
META.DESCRIPTION: A browser extension wallet connects your crypto to dApps in Chrome or Brave. See how it talks to sites, where your key sits, and how to keep it offline.

BROWSER_EXTENSION_WALLET.DEF: A browser extension wallet is a wallet installed in the browser, such as Chrome or Brave. It adds a provider to web pages so dApps can read your address, request a connection and ask for signatures.
BROWSER_EXTENSION_WALLET.WHY: Extensions are the most convenient way to use DeFi, and the most exposed. A traditional extension keeps an encrypted key in the browser profile, next to every other extension and every site you visit. A malicious update or a compromised computer can reach it.
BROWSER_EXTENSION_WALLET.LOCKER: Locker Protocol Wallet is an extension for Chrome and Brave that announces itself to dApps like any other but stores no private key. Each request becomes a QR code signed on Locker Vault, an offline device.

Q1.Q: Are browser extension wallets safe?
Q1.A: The software can be well built and still run on a computer you cannot fully trust. The risk depends on where the key is: in the browser, a compromise can reach it; on a separate offline device, it cannot.

Q2.Q: How does a dApp find my extension wallet?
Q2.A: Through standards: on EVM networks the extension announces itself with EIP-6963, on Solana and Sui through the Wallet Standard, on Aptos through AIP-62. The site lists every wallet it finds in its connect menu.

NON_CUSTODIAL_WALLET.NAME: Non-custodial wallet
NON_CUSTODIAL_WALLET.TITLE: What is a non-custodial wallet?

META.TITLE: What Is a Non-Custodial Wallet? Self-Custody Explained
META.DESCRIPTION: In a non-custodial wallet, you alone hold the keys: no company can freeze or lose your funds. Learn what self-custody means and what it asks of you.

NON_CUSTODIAL_WALLET.DEF: A non-custodial, or self-custody, wallet is one where you hold the private keys yourself. No company can freeze, move or lose your funds, and no one can restore access for you if you lose your recovery phrase.
NON_CUSTODIAL_WALLET.WHY: Exchanges that held their customers' keys have failed or frozen withdrawals, taking customer funds with them. Self-custody removes that risk and replaces it with another: you become responsible for keeping the key safe and the recovery phrase backed up.
NON_CUSTODIAL_WALLET.LOCKER: Locker Protocol Wallet is non-custodial, and goes one step further: even the extension on your computer does not hold the key. Locker Protocol never sees your recovery phrase, and the Vault that holds it never connects to the internet.

Q1.Q: What is the difference between custodial and non-custodial?
Q1.A: Custodial: a company holds the keys and you hold an account with it. Non-custodial: you hold the keys, and the funds are yours on the chain whatever happens to the company that made the wallet.

Q2.Q: What happens to my funds if Locker Protocol disappears?
Q2.A: They stay on the chains, controlled by your recovery phrase. You can restore that phrase in another wallet that supports the same standard (BIP-39).

SEED_PHRASE.NAME: Seed phrase
SEED_PHRASE.TITLE: What is a seed phrase?

META.TITLE: What Is a Seed Phrase? Recovery Phrase Explained
META.DESCRIPTION: A seed phrase is 12 or 24 words that can recreate every key in your wallet. Learn how it works, where to keep it, and the mistakes that empty wallets.

SEED_PHRASE.DEF: A seed phrase, also called a recovery phrase or mnemonic, is a list of 12 or 24 words that encodes the master secret of a wallet. Every private key and address in the wallet is derived from it, on every chain.
SEED_PHRASE.WHY: The phrase is the wallet. Anyone who reads it can recreate your keys on their own device and move everything, with no password to stop them. Most losses come from a phrase typed into a fake site, saved in a photo or a cloud note, or kept on a computer.
SEED_PHRASE.LOCKER: With Locker Protocol Wallet, the phrase is created and kept on Locker Vault, offline, and never typed into the browser. Write it on paper and store it somewhere safe: it is the only way to restore your accounts if the device is lost.

Q1.Q: Should I store my seed phrase in a password manager?
Q1.A: It is safer on paper or metal, offline. A password manager syncs to the cloud and runs on online devices, the exact places attackers look.

Q2.Q: Can I import an existing seed phrase into Locker Vault?
Q2.A: You can, but a phrase that has lived in a browser extension may already have been exposed. We recommend creating a new one on the offline device and moving your funds to it.

PRIVATE_KEY.NAME: Private key
PRIVATE_KEY.TITLE: What is a private key in crypto?

META.TITLE: What Is a Private Key in Crypto? Keys vs Addresses
META.DESCRIPTION: A private key is the secret number that controls one crypto address. Learn how it relates to your address and seed phrase, and why it must stay offline.

PRIVATE_KEY.DEF: A private key is a secret number that controls one address on one blockchain. It produces the signatures that authorise transactions. From it anyone can compute the public key and the address, but not the other way round.
PRIVATE_KEY.WHY: Signing requires the private key, so any software that signs for you has to hold it somewhere. Where decides your security: in a browser, it is one compromise away from theft; on an offline device, an attacker would first have to take the device and learn your master password.
PRIVATE_KEY.LOCKER: Locker Vault derives your private keys from your recovery phrase and keeps them encrypted with your master password, on a device that stays offline. The extension only ever sees public keys and addresses, and revealing a key on the Vault asks for the password every time.

Q1.Q: Is a private key the same as a seed phrase?
Q1.A: No. The seed phrase generates many private keys, one per address and chain. Losing one private key exposes one address; losing the phrase exposes all of them.

Q2.Q: Can someone guess my private key?
Q2.A: Not by chance: the number of possible keys is far beyond anything a computer can search. Keys are stolen, not guessed, which is why where they are stored matters.

WALLET_ADDRESS.NAME: Wallet address
WALLET_ADDRESS.TITLE: What is a crypto wallet address?

META.TITLE: What Is a Crypto Wallet Address? Formats by Chain
META.DESCRIPTION: A wallet address is your public identifier on a blockchain, safe to share. See address formats on Ethereum, Bitcoin and Solana, and how to check them.

WALLET_ADDRESS.DEF: A wallet address is the public identifier others use to send you funds, derived from your public key. It is safe to share. Formats differ by chain: 0x... on Ethereum and EVM networks, bc1... on Bitcoin, T... on Tron, a base58 string on Solana.
WALLET_ADDRESS.WHY: Transactions cannot be undone, so an address typed or pasted wrongly means funds sent to someone else. Attackers exploit this with clipboard malware and with look-alike addresses that match the first and last characters of one you use.
WALLET_ADDRESS.LOCKER: Locker Protocol Wallet shows your addresses on every supported chain from one recovery phrase. When you send, it warns you if the recipient looks like an address you know but differs, and the Vault shows the full recipient again before you sign.

Q1.Q: Is it safe to share my wallet address?
Q1.A: Yes: it lets people send to you, not spend. Anyone who has it can also see the address's balance and history on the chain.

Q2.Q: Why do I have different addresses on different chains?
Q2.A: Each chain family uses its own key type and format. EVM networks share one address, while Bitcoin, Solana, Cosmos, Tron and others each have their own, all derived from the same phrase.

WATCH_ONLY_WALLET.NAME: Watch-only wallet
WATCH_ONLY_WALLET.TITLE: What is a watch-only wallet?

META.TITLE: What Is a Watch-Only Wallet? View Without Keys
META.DESCRIPTION: A watch-only wallet tracks balances from addresses alone, with no private key. Learn how it pairs with an offline signer to keep your key off the internet.

WATCH_ONLY_WALLET.DEF: A watch-only wallet knows your addresses or public keys but not your private keys. It can show balances, history and incoming payments, and prepare transactions, but it cannot sign them.
WATCH_ONLY_WALLET.WHY: It separates looking from spending. The device you use every day, the one exposed to the internet, gets everything it needs to be useful and nothing that could move your funds if it were compromised.
WATCH_ONLY_WALLET.LOCKER: Every account in the Locker Protocol Wallet extension is watch-only: it comes from Locker Vault by QR code and carries public keys only. Transactions prepared in the extension go back to the Vault to be signed. On Bitcoin, the watch-only view can also be exported to Sparrow or Nunchuk.

Q1.Q: Can a watch-only wallet be hacked?
Q1.A: Its data can be read, which reveals balances and addresses, but a thief cannot spend from it because the private keys are not there.

Q2.Q: What is the difference between watch-only and cold storage?
Q2.A: They are two halves of one setup: the cold device keeps the keys and signs, the watch-only wallet shows the funds and prepares transactions online.

QR_CODE_SIGNING.NAME: QR code signing
QR_CODE_SIGNING.TITLE: What is QR code signing?

META.TITLE: What Is QR Code Signing? Air-Gapped Transactions
META.DESCRIPTION: QR code signing moves a transaction to an offline device and back as QR codes, with no cable or Bluetooth. See the four steps and what each device checks.

QR_CODE_SIGNING.DEF: QR code signing is a way to sign a transaction on an offline device without any data link. The unsigned transaction is shown as a QR code on the online computer, scanned by the offline device, signed there, and returned as another QR code.
QR_CODE_SIGNING.WHY: A cable or a Bluetooth link is a channel that malware could use. A camera reading a QR code carries only the data on screen, in one direction at a time, and you see every exchange happen.
QR_CODE_SIGNING.LOCKER: Every signature in Locker Protocol Wallet follows the same loop: the extension shows a request QR, Locker Vault reads it, decodes the transaction and shows it to you, then displays the signed QR, which the extension reads back. Large payloads travel as animated QR codes (BC-UR).

Q1.Q: Is QR signing slower than a hardware wallet?
Q1.A: A few seconds more: two scans per signature. In exchange, you read the transaction on a full phone screen rather than a small device display.

Q2.Q: Can a malicious QR code harm the offline device?
Q2.A: The Vault treats every QR code as data: it decodes it, shows you what it found, and signs nothing until you approve on its screen.

BLIND_SIGNING.NAME: Blind signing
BLIND_SIGNING.TITLE: What is blind signing?

META.TITLE: What Is Blind Signing? The Risk of Unreadable Data
META.DESCRIPTION: Blind signing means approving a transaction your wallet cannot decode. Learn why drainers rely on it and how clear signing shows what you really approve.

BLIND_SIGNING.DEF: Blind signing means approving a transaction or message that your wallet cannot show in readable form, only as a hash or raw hexadecimal data. You sign without knowing what it does.
BLIND_SIGNING.WHY: Most drainer attacks depend on it. A fake site asks for a signature that looks routine but in fact grants a contract permission to move your tokens. If the wallet cannot decode it, you have no way to notice.
BLIND_SIGNING.LOCKER: Locker Vault decodes what it signs on its own screen: contract calls, token approvals, typed data (EIP-712), Bitcoin PSBTs, Cosmos SignDocs. It works out the risk facts from the raw payload itself, so a compromised extension cannot pass a harmful transaction off as harmless.

Q1.Q: Why do some hardware wallets ask for blind signing?
Q1.A: Some cannot parse every smart contract, especially on small screens, so they offer a setting to sign data they cannot decode. It works, but it hands the decision back to trust.

Q2.Q: What is clear signing?
Q2.A: The opposite: the wallet decodes the request and shows who receives what, which token, and which permission is granted, before you approve.

MESSAGE_SIGNING.NAME: Message signing
MESSAGE_SIGNING.TITLE: What is message signing in crypto?

META.TITLE: What Is Message Signing? Sign-In With Ethereum
META.DESCRIPTION: Signing a message moves no funds but proves you own an address, often to log in. Learn when it is harmless, when it is not, and what to check first.

MESSAGE_SIGNING.DEF: Message signing is using your private key to sign text rather than a transaction. It moves nothing on the chain. Sites use it to prove you own an address, for example to log in with Sign-In with Ethereum (EIP-4361).
MESSAGE_SIGNING.WHY: A plain login message is harmless. But signatures can also authorise things off-chain: a gasless token permit or an exchange order is a signed message too, and it can be used later to move your funds.
MESSAGE_SIGNING.LOCKER: Locker Protocol Wallet checks Sign-In with Ethereum requests: a login message that names another site than the one asking is refused, since that is how a fake site opens a session on the real one. Every message, like every transaction, is signed on Locker Vault after you read it there.

Q1.Q: Can signing a message drain my wallet?
Q1.A: A plain text message cannot. A typed-data signature such as a permit can authorise a transfer later, which is why a wallet must show you exactly what the message contains.

Q2.Q: Does message signing cost gas?
Q2.A: No. The signature is made on your device and sent to the site, not to the blockchain.

EIP_712.NAME: EIP-712 (typed data)
EIP_712.TITLE: What is EIP-712 typed data signing?

META.TITLE: What Is EIP-712? Typed Data Signatures Explained
META.DESCRIPTION: EIP-712 lets dApps ask for structured signatures such as permits and orders. Learn what typed data contains and why reading it before you sign matters.

EIP_712.DEF: EIP-712 is an Ethereum standard for signing structured data instead of plain text. The request lists named fields, such as a spender, an amount and a deadline, under a domain that names the contract and the chain it is meant for.
EIP_712.WHY: Typed data powers gasless approvals (Permit, Permit2), exchange orders and many dApp logins. Because it can authorise token transfers without an on-chain transaction, it is a favourite of phishing sites: one signature can hand over a token balance.
EIP_712.LOCKER: Locker Vault decodes EIP-712 requests field by field, and its risk checks flag permits and Permit2 approvals. Locker Protocol's own contracts use typed data too, so each operation you sign is readable on the offline screen.

Q1.Q: Is signing EIP-712 data safe?
Q1.A: It depends on the content. Read the domain (which contract, which chain), the spender and the amount. An unlimited permit to an unknown address is the classic drainer pattern.

Q2.Q: Does EIP-712 cost gas?
Q2.A: Signing does not. The dApp may later submit the signature on-chain, and that transaction pays the fee.

TOKEN_APPROVAL.NAME: Token approval
TOKEN_APPROVAL.TITLE: What is a token approval?

META.TITLE: What Is a Token Approval? Allowances and Revoking
META.DESCRIPTION: A token approval lets a contract move your tokens, sometimes without limit. Learn how allowances work, why unlimited ones are risky, and how to revoke.

TOKEN_APPROVAL.DEF: A token approval, or allowance, is a permission you give a smart contract to move up to a set amount of one of your tokens. dApps need it before they can swap or deposit your tokens for you.
TOKEN_APPROVAL.WHY: Many dApps ask for an unlimited approval so you never have to approve again. That permission stays valid until you revoke it. If the contract is malicious, or is exploited later, it can take every token of that kind in your wallet, at any time.
TOKEN_APPROVAL.LOCKER: Locker Protocol Wallet flags unlimited approvals, collection-wide NFT approvals (setApprovalForAll) and Permit2 before you sign, in the extension and again on the Vault. Its Revoke screen cancels an allowance; the revocation is a transaction signed on the Vault.

Q1.Q: Should I revoke old token approvals?
Q1.A: Yes, for contracts you no longer use. Revoking costs a small network fee and removes a permission that could be abused later.

Q2.Q: What is the difference between approve and setApprovalForAll?
Q2.A: approve covers one token up to an amount. setApprovalForAll covers every NFT of a collection you own, now and later, which makes it a frequent target of NFT scams.

WALLET_DRAINER.NAME: Wallet drainer
WALLET_DRAINER.TITLE: What is a crypto wallet drainer?

META.TITLE: What Is a Wallet Drainer? How Drainers Steal Crypto
META.DESCRIPTION: A wallet drainer is a script on a fake site that tricks you into signing away your tokens. See how drainers work and the signatures they ask for.

WALLET_DRAINER.DEF: A wallet drainer is malicious code, usually on a fake or hacked website, that asks your wallet for signatures designed to transfer your assets to the attacker. It is sold as a ready-made kit, which is why drainer sites appear by the thousand.
WALLET_DRAINER.WHY: Drainers do not need your key. They need you to approve: an unlimited token approval, a permit, a setApprovalForAll, or on Solana a transaction that hands over authority on your accounts. The request is dressed up as a mint, an airdrop claim or a login.
WALLET_DRAINER.LOCKER: Locker Protocol Wallet checks the site against a bundled list of about 105,000 known phishing hosts when it connects, flags drainer patterns such as unlimited approvals, EIP-7702 delegations and Solana SetAuthority, and shows the decoded transaction on the offline Vault before anything is signed.

Q1.Q: Can a drainer empty a hardware wallet?
Q1.A: Yes, if you approve its request. A hardware wallet protects the key, not your judgement, so what counts is whether the device shows you what the signature does.

Q2.Q: What should I do if I signed a drainer request?
Q2.A: Revoke the approvals you gave at once, and move the remaining funds to a new address from a recovery phrase that was never exposed.

PHISHING.NAME: Crypto phishing
PHISHING.TITLE: What is crypto phishing?

META.TITLE: What Is Crypto Phishing? Fake Sites and Signatures
META.DESCRIPTION: Crypto phishing imitates real sites, apps and support to steal seed phrases or signatures. Learn the common tricks and how a wallet can warn you in time.

PHISHING.DEF: Crypto phishing is any fake site, message, ad or app that imitates a real one to make you reveal your recovery phrase or sign a harmful transaction. Look-alike domains, fake support accounts and sponsored search results are common routes.
PHISHING.WHY: A phishing page can be a pixel-perfect copy of a real dApp. The only differences may be one character in the domain and what the signature request actually does, both easy to miss.
PHISHING.LOCKER: Locker Protocol Wallet warns you when you connect to a site on its bundled phishing list, or to a domain written with unusual characters (punycode). The warning is advisory and the decision stays yours; every request is then decoded again on the Vault.

Q1.Q: Will a real wallet ever ask for my seed phrase?
Q1.A: No. No support team, dApp or update needs your recovery phrase. Anyone who asks for it is trying to take your funds.

Q2.Q: How do I spot a phishing site?
Q2.A: Type the address yourself or use a bookmark, check the domain letter by letter, and distrust urgency: a mint ending in minutes, a claim about to expire, a security alert.

ADDRESS_POISONING.NAME: Address poisoning
ADDRESS_POISONING.TITLE: What is address poisoning?

META.TITLE: What Is Address Poisoning? Look-Alike Address Scam
META.DESCRIPTION: Address poisoning plants a look-alike address in your history so you copy it by mistake. Learn how the scam works and how to check a recipient.

ADDRESS_POISONING.DEF: Address poisoning is a scam in which an attacker sends you a tiny amount, or a fake token transfer, from an address that starts and ends like one you use. The hope is that you will later copy it from your history and send funds to it.
ADDRESS_POISONING.WHY: Most people check only the first and last few characters of an address. Attackers generate addresses that match exactly those characters, so the poisoned entry looks right at a glance.
ADDRESS_POISONING.LOCKER: When you send, Locker Protocol Wallet compares the recipient with the addresses you have used and warns you if it looks like one of them but differs, asking you to check every character. The Vault shows the full recipient again before you sign.

Q1.Q: Has my wallet been hacked if I receive a poisoned transfer?
Q1.A: No. Receiving it does no harm. The danger is only in copying that address later: ignore it, or hide the fake token.

Q2.Q: How do I protect myself from address poisoning?
Q2.A: Keep the addresses you use in your contacts, never copy a recipient from your transaction history, and compare the full address on the signing device.

GAS_FEE.NAME: Gas fee
GAS_FEE.TITLE: What is a gas fee?

META.TITLE: What Is a Gas Fee? Network Fees in Crypto Explained
META.DESCRIPTION: A gas fee is what you pay a blockchain to process your transaction, in its own coin. Learn how fees are set, why they vary, and what a low fee does.

GAS_FEE.DEF: A gas fee, or network fee, is what you pay the network's validators to include your transaction. It is paid in the chain's own coin (ETH on Ethereum, SOL on Solana, TRX on Tron) and depends on how much work the transaction needs and how busy the network is.
GAS_FEE.WHY: Without enough of the native coin you cannot move anything, not even a stablecoin. A fee set too low can leave a transaction pending; one set carelessly high wastes money.
GAS_FEE.LOCKER: Before preparing a send or a swap, Locker Protocol Wallet checks that you hold enough of the asset and enough native coin for the fee, and tells you when you do not. A pending EVM transaction can be sped up or cancelled with a replacement signed on the Vault.

Q1.Q: Why do I need ETH to send USDC?
Q1.A: Because the network is paid in its own coin. The token you send and the coin that pays the fee are two different balances.

Q2.Q: Does Locker Protocol Wallet add a fee on sends?
Q2.A: No. A send costs only the network fee. The wallet's own fee applies to swaps and bridges made in the extension (at most 0.25%), and it is shown before you sign.

NONCE.NAME: Nonce
NONCE.TITLE: What is a nonce in a crypto transaction?

META.TITLE: What Is a Transaction Nonce? Speed Up and Cancel
META.DESCRIPTION: A nonce is the sequence number of a transaction from your account. Learn why a stuck transaction blocks the next ones and how speed up and cancel work.

NONCE.DEF: On Ethereum and EVM networks, the nonce is the sequence number of a transaction sent from an account: 0 for the first, then 1, 2 and so on. Each nonce can be used only once, and transactions are processed in order.
NONCE.WHY: If one transaction is stuck, every later one waits behind it. The only way to replace it is to send another with the same nonce and a higher fee: the same transaction, faster (speed up), or a zero-value transfer to yourself (cancel).
NONCE.LOCKER: Locker Protocol Wallet offers speed up and cancel on pending EVM transactions. The replacement is a new transaction with the same nonce, prepared by the extension and signed again on Locker Vault.

Q1.Q: Why is my transaction stuck as pending?
Q1.A: Usually the fee was too low for current demand, or an earlier transaction with a lower nonce has not gone through yet.

Q2.Q: Can I cancel a confirmed transaction?
Q2.A: No. Speed up and cancel only work while the transaction is pending. Once it is confirmed on the chain, it is final.

DAPP.NAME: dApp
DAPP.TITLE: What is a dApp?

META.TITLE: What Is a dApp? Decentralized Apps and Your Wallet
META.DESCRIPTION: A dApp is a website or app that runs on blockchain smart contracts and connects to your wallet. See how connecting works and what a dApp can and cannot do.

DAPP.DEF: A dApp, or decentralized application, is an app, usually a website, whose logic runs in smart contracts on a blockchain. You connect a wallet to it to trade, lend, stake, vote or mint.
DAPP.WHY: Connecting shares your address with the site. It does not give the site access to your funds: every action still needs a signature. The risk lies in what you sign, and in whether the site is the real one.
DAPP.LOCKER: Locker Protocol Wallet has been tested against more than 70 live dApps across its chains, among them Jupiter, Osmosis, Lido and SunSwap. You connect as usual, and each signature is approved on the offline Vault.

Q1.Q: Is connecting my wallet to a dApp safe?
Q1.A: Connecting alone moves nothing. Be careful with what you sign afterwards, and remove the sites you no longer use from the wallet's list of connected sites.

Q2.Q: Which dApps work with Locker Protocol Wallet?
Q2.A: Our dApp directory lists every site checked against its live version, with the date of the test and the button to pick in the site's menu.

SWAP.NAME: Crypto swap
SWAP.TITLE: What is a crypto swap?

META.TITLE: What Is a Crypto Swap? Fees, Slippage and Routes
META.DESCRIPTION: A crypto swap trades one token for another on the same network through a decentralized exchange. Learn how routes, slippage and fees shape your price.

SWAP.DEF: A swap trades one token for another on the same blockchain, through a decentralized exchange or an aggregator that splits the order across several of them. It settles in a single transaction that you sign.
SWAP.WHY: The price you get depends on liquidity, on the route and on slippage, the price movement you accept between the quote and the execution. Loose slippage invites front-running, and hidden fees reduce what you receive.
SWAP.LOCKER: Locker Protocol Wallet includes a swap in the extension. The quote and the wallet's fee, at most 0.25%, are shown before you sign on the Vault.

Q1.Q: What is slippage?
Q1.A: The difference you accept between the quoted price and the executed price. If the market moves more than that, the swap fails instead of filling at a worse price.

Q2.Q: Is swapping in a wallet more expensive than on a DEX?
Q2.A: Wallets often add a fee on top of the exchange's. Compare the amount you receive, not only the headline rate. Locker's fee is shown before you sign.

BRIDGE.NAME: Crypto bridge
BRIDGE.TITLE: What is a crypto bridge?

META.TITLE: What Is a Crypto Bridge? Moving Tokens Across Chains
META.DESCRIPTION: A crypto bridge moves value from one blockchain to another. Learn how bridges work, how long a transfer takes, and why it cannot be recalled.

BRIDGE.DEF: A bridge moves value from one blockchain to another, for example USDC from Ethereum to Solana. Depending on the design, it locks tokens on one side and releases them on the other, or pays you from liquidity already waiting on the destination chain.
BRIDGE.WHY: Bridges hold large pools of funds, which makes them prime targets for hacks. A transfer usually takes minutes, cannot be recalled once sent, and you need a little native coin on the destination chain to use what arrives.
BRIDGE.LOCKER: Locker Protocol Wallet includes bridging in the extension, between the chains it supports. The destination and the wallet's fee (at most 0.25%) are shown before you sign on the Vault, and the transfer is followed until it lands.

Q1.Q: How long does a bridge transfer take?
Q1.A: From under a minute to about half an hour, depending on the route and on how many confirmations the source chain requires.

Q2.Q: What if my bridged tokens do not arrive?
Q2.A: Look up the transfer on the bridge's explorer with the source transaction hash. Most delays resolve on their own; a transfer sent to the wrong chain or address cannot be reversed.

PERPS.NAME: Perpetual futures
PERPS.TITLE: What are perpetual futures (perps)?

META.TITLE: What Are Perpetual Futures? Perps and Leverage
META.DESCRIPTION: Perpetual futures let you bet on a price with leverage and no expiry date. Learn how funding, margin and liquidation work, and the risks involved.

PERPS.DEF: Perpetual futures, or perps, are contracts that track the price of an asset without ever expiring. You open a long or short position with margin and optional leverage; a funding rate paid between longs and shorts keeps the contract close to the spot price.
PERPS.WHY: Leverage multiplies gains and losses. If the price moves far enough against you, the position is liquidated and you can lose the whole margin. Perps are for traders who accept that risk, not for savings.
PERPS.LOCKER: Locker Protocol Wallet can trade perps on Hyperliquid through an agent key: a time-limited key that may place orders for you but can never withdraw. Deposits and withdrawals are signed on the Vault. The wallet charges 0.05% on Hyperliquid orders once you approve it.

Q1.Q: What is liquidation?
Q1.A: The forced closing of a position when your margin no longer covers the loss. It happens automatically at the liquidation price.

Q2.Q: What is a funding rate?
Q2.A: A periodic payment between long and short traders that keeps the perp price near the market price. Depending on its sign, you pay it or receive it while the position is open.

PSBT.NAME: PSBT
PSBT.TITLE: What is a PSBT in Bitcoin?

META.TITLE: What Is a PSBT? Partially Signed Bitcoin Transactions
META.DESCRIPTION: A PSBT is the standard format for passing an unsigned Bitcoin transaction to a signer. Learn what it contains and what an offline signer should check.

PSBT.DEF: A PSBT (Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction, BIP-174) is the standard format for handing an unsigned Bitcoin transaction from one tool to another. It carries the inputs, the outputs and the data a signer needs, and collects signatures until the transaction is complete.
PSBT.WHY: It is what lets a watch-only wallet and an offline signer work together. The signer must decode it itself: the outputs and the fee are exactly what a tampered PSBT would change.
PSBT.LOCKER: Locker Protocol Wallet builds the PSBT in the extension and passes it to Locker Vault by QR code. The Vault decodes it itself: every output, the fee as a share of the amount, outputs below the dust limit, and inputs this wallet does not control.

Q1.Q: Is a PSBT safe to share?
Q1.A: It holds no private key, so whoever sees it cannot spend with it. It does reveal your addresses and amounts, so share it only with your own tools.

Q2.Q: Does a PSBT work with Taproot?
Q2.A: Yes. PSBTs carry Native SegWit and Taproot inputs, both of which Locker Protocol Wallet uses on Bitcoin.

BC_UR.NAME: BC-UR
BC_UR.TITLE: What is BC-UR?

META.TITLE: What Is BC-UR? Animated QR Codes for Wallets
META.DESCRIPTION: BC-UR is an open standard for passing wallet data through QR codes, animated when it is large. Learn why air-gapped wallets use it and how it stays robust.

BC_UR.DEF: BC-UR (Uniform Resources, from Blockchain Commons) is a standard for encoding binary data such as transactions, PSBTs and account keys into QR codes. When the data is too large for one code, it is split into an animated sequence of frames.
BC_UR.WHY: A single QR code holds a few kilobytes at most, and dense codes are hard to scan. BC-UR uses fountain codes: the reader can rebuild the payload from any sufficient set of frames, so a missed frame costs a moment, not a restart.
BC_UR.LOCKER: Locker Protocol Wallet and Locker Vault exchange large requests as BC-UR animated QR codes, the family of formats also used by Keystone and other air-gapped wallets. The Vault caps the size of what it will assemble before it decodes anything.

Q1.Q: Why does the QR code keep changing?
Q1.A: It is an animated sequence carrying a payload too large for one code. Hold the camera on it until the Vault reports it has read everything.

Q2.Q: Is BC-UR tied to one wallet brand?
Q2.A: No. It is an open specification from Blockchain Commons, used by several hardware and software wallets.

ORDINALS.NAME: Bitcoin Ordinals
ORDINALS.TITLE: What are Bitcoin Ordinals?

META.TITLE: What Are Bitcoin Ordinals? Inscriptions on Sats
META.DESCRIPTION: Ordinals number individual satoshis so data can be inscribed on them, creating Bitcoin NFTs. Learn how inscriptions work and how to avoid spending one.

ORDINALS.DEF: Ordinals is a scheme that numbers each satoshi, the smallest unit of bitcoin, so it can be tracked individually. Data inscribed on a satoshi (an image, text, a token) is called an inscription and is often described as a Bitcoin NFT.
ORDINALS.WHY: To Bitcoin itself, an inscribed satoshi is ordinary money. A wallet that ignores Ordinals can spend it as a fee or send it along with a payment, and the inscription is gone for good.
ORDINALS.LOCKER: Locker Vault keeps Ordinals on a Taproot address separate from your payment funds, so ordinary sends do not spend inscriptions by accident. Ordinals marketplaces such as Satflow and Best in Slot connect through the extension.

Q1.Q: What are Runes?
Q1.A: A Bitcoin standard for fungible tokens, launched in 2024. Unlike Ordinals, which track individual satoshis, Runes balances are recorded in transaction outputs.

Q2.Q: Do I need a special wallet for Ordinals?
Q2.A: You need one that knows which outputs carry inscriptions and keeps them apart. A plain Bitcoin wallet may spend them without warning.

TRUSTLINE.NAME: Trustline
TRUSTLINE.TITLE: What is a trustline on Stellar and XRP?

META.TITLE: What Is a Trustline? Stellar and XRP Ledger Assets
META.DESCRIPTION: A trustline lets your account hold a token on Stellar or the XRP Ledger, and it locks a small reserve. Learn how to add one and what it costs.

TRUSTLINE.DEF: On Stellar and the XRP Ledger, a trustline is your account's agreement to hold a specific asset from a specific issuer, such as USDC. Until you add one, the account cannot receive that asset.
TRUSTLINE.WHY: Each trustline locks a small amount of the native coin (XLM or XRP) as reserve. Trusting a fake issuer that uses the same asset code is a common scam: what matters is the issuer's address, not the ticker.
TRUSTLINE.LOCKER: Locker Protocol Wallet names the reserve a trustline locks before you approve it, and the offline Vault shows the trustline in full when it signs.

Q1.Q: Why can't I receive USDC on Stellar?
Q1.A: Your account first needs a trustline to Circle's USDC issuer. Adding it is a small transaction and locks a little XLM as reserve.

Q2.Q: Can I remove a trustline?
Q2.A: Yes, once its balance is zero. Removing it releases the reserve it locked.

MEMO.NAME: Memo and destination tag
MEMO.TITLE: What is a memo or destination tag?

META.TITLE: Memo and Destination Tag: Why Exchanges Need Them
META.DESCRIPTION: A memo or destination tag tells an exchange whose deposit a payment is. Learn when Stellar, Cosmos and XRP need it, and what happens without it.

MEMO.DEF: A memo is a short note attached to a payment on Stellar and the Cosmos chains; on the XRP Ledger the same role is played by a number called a destination tag. Exchanges use one shared address for many customers and rely on it to credit the right account.
MEMO.WHY: Forget it when depositing to an exchange and the funds reach the exchange's address with no owner attached; getting them back means a support ticket at best. On THORChain the memo is not a note at all: it is the instruction that tells the protocol what to do.
MEMO.LOCKER: Locker Protocol Wallet lets you enter the memo or destination tag when you send, and the Vault shows it as part of the payment before signing, so a missing or wrong one is visible before the funds leave.

Q1.Q: Do I need a memo to send to my own wallet?
Q1.A: Usually not. Personal addresses do not need one; exchange deposit addresses usually do, and say so on their deposit page.

Q2.Q: What if I sent funds without a memo?
Q2.A: Contact the exchange's support with the transaction hash. They can often credit it by hand, but it can take days.

IBC.NAME: IBC
IBC.TITLE: What is IBC in Cosmos?

META.TITLE: What Is IBC? Inter-Blockchain Communication in Cosmos
META.DESCRIPTION: IBC is the protocol Cosmos chains use to move tokens between each other. Learn how channels work, what IBC denoms are, and how to send ATOM to Osmosis.

IBC.DEF: IBC (Inter-Blockchain Communication) is the protocol Cosmos chains use to send tokens and messages to each other, over a port and a channel opened between two chains. A token that crosses over appears on the other side under an ibc/... denomination.
IBC.WHY: Choosing the wrong channel, or sending to an address on the wrong chain, can leave tokens stranded. Each chain has its own address prefix (cosmos1..., osmo1..., inj1...), all derived from the same key.
IBC.LOCKER: Locker Protocol Wallet covers the Cosmos chains it supports, among them Osmosis, Injective and Stride, from one recovery phrase. The Vault decodes the SignDoc itself and shows every message before you sign.

Q1.Q: What is an IBC denom?
Q1.A: The name a token carries on a chain it was sent to, such as ibc/27394FB0... for ATOM on Osmosis. It is a hash of the path the token travelled.

Q2.Q: Is IBC a bridge?
Q2.A: It plays the same role between Cosmos chains, but it is a native protocol checked by each chain's light clients rather than a separate service holding the funds.

AUTHZ.NAME: authz grant
AUTHZ.TITLE: What is an authz grant in Cosmos?

META.TITLE: What Is an Authz Grant? Cosmos Permissions Explained
META.DESCRIPTION: An authz grant lets another Cosmos account act for yours, such as restaking rewards. Learn when grants help, when they are a trap, and how to revoke one.

AUTHZ.DEF: authz is a Cosmos SDK module that lets one account (the granter) authorise another (the grantee) to send certain messages on its behalf, within limits and until an expiry date. Auto-compounding services use it to restake rewards for you.
AUTHZ.WHY: A broad grant, such as a generic authorization to send tokens, lets the grantee move your funds without asking again. Phishing sites disguise such grants as routine staking actions.
AUTHZ.LOCKER: Locker Vault shows an authz grant in red on its review screen, so it cannot pass as an ordinary signature. Read who receives the permission and what it covers before you approve.

Q1.Q: How do I revoke an authz grant?
Q1.A: Send a revoke message (MsgRevoke) for that grantee and message type, from a staking dashboard that supports it. It is a regular transaction and costs a small fee.

Q2.Q: Are authz grants always dangerous?
Q2.A: No. A narrow grant, limited to restaking with a validator you chose and with an expiry date, is how auto-compounding works. The danger lies in broad or permanent grants to accounts you do not know.

MULTICHAIN_WALLET.NAME: Multichain wallet
MULTICHAIN_WALLET.TITLE: What is a multichain wallet?

META.TITLE: What Is a Multichain Wallet? One Phrase, Many Chains
META.DESCRIPTION: A multichain wallet holds assets on several blockchains from one recovery phrase. Learn how it works and what to check: chains, dApp support and signing.

MULTICHAIN_WALLET.DEF: A multichain wallet manages accounts on several blockchains, such as Ethereum, Solana and Bitcoin, from a single recovery phrase. Each chain family gets its own keys and address format, all derived from the same seed.
MULTICHAIN_WALLET.WHY: One wallet for everything is simpler to use and to back up. The catch: one phrase then protects everything, and support varies. A wallet may list a chain but not connect to its dApps, or show a balance it cannot sign for.
MULTICHAIN_WALLET.LOCKER: Locker Protocol Wallet covers EVM networks, Solana, Bitcoin, Litecoin, Dogecoin, Cosmos chains, Tron, Sui, Aptos, Stellar and the XRP Ledger from one phrase kept on Locker Vault, and connects to dApps through each chain's own standard.

Q1.Q: Is a multichain wallet less secure?
Q1.A: Not in itself. Security depends on where the phrase and the keys live. One phrase on an offline device protects every chain equally.

Q2.Q: Can I use the same address on every chain?
Q2.A: Only on EVM networks, which share one address format. Other chains each have their own addresses.

TOKEN_LOCKER.NAME: Token locker
TOKEN_LOCKER.TITLE: What is a token locker?

META.TITLE: What Is a Token Locker? Liquidity Locks and Vesting
META.DESCRIPTION: A token locker is a smart contract that holds tokens until a date or a price, to lock liquidity or vest a team's allocation. Learn how locks build trust.

TOKEN_LOCKER.DEF: A token locker is a smart contract that holds tokens and releases them only under set conditions: a date, a price or a vesting schedule. Projects use it to lock liquidity pool tokens or team allocations so they cannot be sold early.
TOKEN_LOCKER.WHY: Buyers of a new token want proof that the team cannot pull the liquidity or dump its allocation overnight. A lock on a public, verified contract is that proof, as long as its owner cannot bypass it.
TOKEN_LOCKER.LOCKER: Locker Protocol started here: its ERC-20 locking contracts support time and price locks, automated vesting and multi-signature control, with every operation signed offline on Locker Vault. The contracts are public and verified on-chain.

Q1.Q: What is a liquidity lock?
Q1.A: Locking the LP tokens of a trading pool in a contract for a set time, so the liquidity cannot be withdrawn, and the token cannot be rug-pulled that way, during the lock.

Q2.Q: What is token vesting?
Q2.A: Releasing an allocation gradually over time, often after a cliff, so holders receive their tokens in steps rather than all at once.

S1.TITLE: Set up the wallet
S1.DESC: Install Locker Protocol Wallet in Chrome or Brave, and Locker Vault on a spare phone kept offline. Your addresses reach the extension by QR code.

S2.TITLE: Receive {{symbol}}
S2.DESC: Give your address on the network the sender uses. The network matters: {{symbol}} sent on one network does not arrive on another.

S3.TITLE: Send {{symbol}}
S3.DESC: Enter the recipient and the amount in the extension and check the network fee, then scan the request with the Vault, read it there and approve.

TOKENS.FEE_NOTE: A transfer is paid in the network's own coin, even when you send a token: keep a little of the coin shown in the table.

NETWORK.Q: Which network should I use to receive {{symbol}}?
NETWORK.A: The one the sender uses. When you withdraw from an exchange, choose the same network in the withdrawal form as the address you give. If they do not match, the funds may not arrive.

FEE.Q: Does Locker Protocol Wallet charge a fee to hold or send {{symbol}}?
FEE.A: No. Holding costs nothing and a transfer costs only the network fee. The wallet's own fee applies to swaps and bridges made in the extension, at most 0.25%, and it is shown before you sign.

FAKE.Q: How do I avoid a fake {{symbol}} token?
FAKE.A: Compare the contract with the one listed here or on the issuer's site. A token that appears in your wallet unasked, calling itself {{symbol}}, is often bait for a scam.

KEY.Q: Where is the private key that controls my {{symbol}}?
KEY.A: On Locker Vault, the offline device, derived from your recovery phrase. The extension on your computer only knows your addresses, so malware there cannot move your {{symbol}}.

USDT.DESC: Tether USD (USDT) is a stablecoin issued by Tether and designed to keep a value of one US dollar. It circulates on many networks, with most of its supply on Tron and Ethereum.

USDC.DESC: USD Coin (USDC) is a stablecoin issued by Circle, backed by cash and short-term US government bonds and redeemable one for one in US dollars. On Arbitrum and Optimism, the older bridged version is listed separately as USDC.e.

DAI.DESC: Dai is a decentralized stablecoin created by the Maker protocol, now Sky, and backed by crypto collateral locked in smart contracts.

USD1.DESC: USD1 is a US dollar stablecoin issued by World Liberty Financial, backed by US Treasuries, cash and cash equivalents.

PYUSD.DESC: PayPal USD (PYUSD) is a US dollar stablecoin issued by Paxos for PayPal and redeemable one for one.

USDE.DESC: USDe is Ethena's synthetic dollar: it stays near one US dollar through crypto collateral hedged with short futures positions, not through bank deposits.

USDG.DESC: Global Dollar (USDG) is a US dollar stablecoin issued by Paxos for the Global Dollar Network.

USDH.DESC: USDH is a US dollar stablecoin native to Hyperliquid, issued by Native Markets.

USDT0.DESC: USDT0 is Tether's USDT in omnichain form, moved between networks through LayerZero. It is the USDT used on HyperEVM.

USDD.DESC: USDD is a stablecoin of the Tron ecosystem, backed by collateral held by the TRON DAO Reserve. It moved to a new contract, and the wallet recognizes both the current one and the first version.

TUSD.DESC: TrueUSD (TUSD) is a US dollar stablecoin, held here as a TRC-20 token on Tron.

GHO.DESC: GHO is the decentralized stablecoin of the Aave protocol, minted by borrowers against the collateral they deposit on Aave.

LUSD.DESC: Liquity USD (LUSD) is a decentralized stablecoin minted against ETH collateral through the Liquity protocol.

WLFI.DESC: WLFI is the governance token of World Liberty Financial, the project that issues the USD1 stablecoin.

ONDO.DESC: ONDO is the governance token of Ondo Finance, a platform for tokenized US Treasuries and other real-world assets.

LINK.DESC: LINK is the token of Chainlink, the oracle network that brings off-chain data such as prices to smart contracts.

ARB.DESC: ARB is the governance token of Arbitrum, the Ethereum layer 2 network, used to vote in the Arbitrum DAO.

OP.DESC: OP is the governance token of Optimism and its Superchain, used to vote in the Optimism Collective.

JST.DESC: JST is the governance token of JUST, a DeFi platform on Tron for lending and stablecoins.

SUN.DESC: SUN is the governance token of SUN.io, the Tron DeFi platform behind SunSwap.

WIN.DESC: WIN is the token of WINkLink, an oracle network on Tron.

BTT.DESC: BTT is the BitTorrent token, used across the BitTorrent ecosystem and its BTTC chain.

HTX.DESC: HTX is the token of HTX DAO, tied to the HTX exchange, formerly Huobi.

WETH.DESC: Wrapped Ether (WETH) is ETH in token form, exchangeable one for one with ETH, so that smart contracts can handle it like any other token.

WBTC.DESC: Wrapped Bitcoin (WBTC) is a token backed one for one by bitcoin held in custody, which brings BTC to Ethereum and other networks.

CBBTC.DESC: Coinbase Wrapped BTC (cbBTC) is a token backed one for one by bitcoin held by Coinbase.

ETH.DESC: Ether (ETH) is the native coin of Ethereum. It pays transaction fees on Ethereum and on the layer 2 networks built on it, such as Arbitrum, Optimism, Base and Linea.

BTC.DESC: Bitcoin (BTC) is the first cryptocurrency, running on its own network since 2009 with a supply capped at 21 million.

SOL.DESC: SOL is the native coin of Solana. It pays transaction fees and is staked to secure the network.

TRX.DESC: TRX is the native coin of Tron. It pays for bandwidth and energy, or can be staked to obtain them.

BNB.DESC: BNB is the native coin of BNB Chain, where it pays transaction fees.

POL.DESC: POL is the native coin of Polygon PoS. It replaced MATIC in 2024.

AVAX.DESC: AVAX is the native coin of Avalanche. It pays fees on the C-Chain, where Avalanche's EVM apps run.

HYPE.DESC: HYPE is the native token of Hyperliquid. It pays gas on HyperEVM and is staked to secure the network.

OSMO.DESC: OSMO is the native token of Osmosis, the Cosmos chain behind the ecosystem's largest decentralized exchange.

INJ.DESC: INJ is the native token of Injective, a Cosmos chain built for finance applications.

RUNE.DESC: RUNE is the native token of THORChain, which swaps native assets across chains, such as BTC for ETH, without wrapping them.

SUI.DESC: SUI is the native coin of Sui. It pays gas fees and is staked to secure the network.

APT.DESC: APT is the native coin of Aptos. It pays gas fees and is staked to secure the network.

XLM.DESC: Lumens (XLM) are the native coin of Stellar. Every account keeps a small XLM reserve, and fees are paid in XLM.

XRP.DESC: XRP is the native coin of the XRP Ledger. Every account keeps a reserve in XRP, and fees are paid in XRP.

LTC.DESC: Litecoin (LTC) is one of the oldest cryptocurrencies, launched in 2011 as a faster sibling of Bitcoin.

DOGE.DESC: Dogecoin (DOGE) started as a joke in 2013 and became one of the most widely held cryptocurrencies.
